result.title_plain: Programme foundation: automatic checks and safety gates
result.purpose_plain: This is the base every later part of the hospital system is built on: the project's folder layout, its planning and safety records, and an automatic checking line that runs on every change. The checks refuse a change if a test fails, if a password or key gets into the code, if a component's licence is not allowed, or if someone fills in a safety approval that a named clinician has not signed. A hospital needs this so that nothing reaches patients on an unchecked claim, and every claim that something passes has a stored record behind it.

showcases.title: The rule the safety gate enforces, as written at the top of the hazard log
showcases.caption: Until a named human adds a signed sign-off record, every safety control stays 'planned' and every risk-acceptance or triage field stays empty. The automated build may never fill them, and the safety check fails the run if anyone does. In this entry format, each of the 21 safety rules is quoted word for word and split into clauses, so the check can prove that every clause has at least one control.
showcases.code:
# Seeded in WP-0.1:
# - seeded_hazards: H1 to H15 as written in BUILD-PROMPT.md §2.4 (BP §5.1);
# - hazards: one entry per safety invariant, SI-01 to SI-21 (HAZ-0001 to HAZ-0021, in SI order),
#   each quoting its invariant verbatim (invariant_text) and split into clauses (invariant_clauses)
#   so that the check can prove every clause is covered by at least one control;
# - HAZ-0022 to HAZ-0027: one entry per SI-21 sensitivity label, because SI-21 says
#   "Each label has its own hazard entry and property tests".
#
# Rules that hold for every entry until a human says otherwise:
# - every control is `planned`, with empty implemented_in and verified_by;
# - initial_risk is an agent proposal for CSO triage [HUMAN], never an acceptance;
# - residual_risk.accepted_by, cso_triage.by, cso_triage.date and every approval field stay null
#   until a human adds a sign-off record under docs/safety/signoffs/ (BUILD-PROMPT §3.5).
#   The agent never fills them.

result.title_plain: The on-site server cell, and its copy on the development laptop
result.purpose_plain: Each hospital will run a small cluster of three servers in its own building, called the "cell". It holds the database, messaging, sign-in and file storage, so the wards keep working when the internet link is down. This work package builds a copy of that cell on the development laptop. Every software image in it is pinned to an exact fingerprint, signed with a local key and served from a local registry. That lets the team prove the cell's safety promises, such as losing one server never losing a saved record, on the same design that hospitals will run.

showcases.title: The lite cell: what is built, what is planned, and why the first try died
showcases.caption: On site, a hospital's cell is three servers. If one fails, the other two carry on and no saved record is lost. The full 'dev cell' copy needs a 32 GB machine. This laptop runs the 'lite cell' instead: three k3s servers as containers inside a 10 GB Linux VM, with one Kafka broker instead of three, three PostgreSQL copies and no Argo CD. Every result from it is labelled 'lite'. Green boxes are code that is written but not committed: the local registry, offline signing and the pin file. Dashed boxes are planned. The servers' fixed addresses are not in any file yet: the first planned range clashed with WSL's own network, so the next step picks one. The bottom panel shows why the first prototype died. WSL shut itself down when idle, which acted as a power cut to all three servers. The servers came back in a different order and swapped addresses (172.18.0.2 and .3). The database that keeps the servers in agreement (etcd) then kept calling the wrong partners, never reached a majority, and the cluster never came back. The planned fix has three parts: fixed addresses, a nightly test that kills all three servers and restarts them in reverse order, and a small 'keeper' process that keeps WSL awake during work sessions. result.title_plain: Core libraries: IDs, clocks, clinical time, money, doses and safe settings
result.purpose_plain: These are the basic building blocks that every other part of the hospital system relies on. They give every record a number that can never clash with another, a clock that tests can control, two separate times on every clinical entry (when it happened and when it was typed in) so late charting always shows, money in Iraqi dinars and US dollars without rounding errors, and doses that cannot be entered without a unit. On top of these sit the settings rules, which let each hospital, ward and user adjust the system but never undo a safety setting the vendor has locked, and a task engine in which no piece of work can be left without an owner.

showcases.title: Late charting is labelled, never hidden
showcases.caption: Every clinical entry carries two times. The first is when it happened, given by the nurse or the device. The second is when the system recorded it, read only from the server's clock. If the gap between them is longer than the allowed window, the entry is not quietly treated as on time: it is labelled back-dated. A back-dated entry needs the back-dating privilege and a reason, keeps both times in the audit trail, and is labelled on screen, in print and in exports. A time too far in the future is refused. The test checks both sides of the window, down to the microsecond. The 5-minute window in the test is a made-up test value. The real windows are for the Clinical Safety Officer to decide, and until then any entry that needs one is refused. The code and the test are uncommitted and have not run yet.

showcases.title: The settings chain and its locks
showcases.caption: A setting can be given a value at eight levels, from the vendor down to a single user, and normally the most specific value wins (left lane). A hospital can lock a setting with an approved change. Below the lock, departments, wards and users cannot override it: an attempt is refused when written, and any override found in storage is ignored (middle lane). Safety settings that the vendor has fixed cannot be set by the Kurdistan pack, the hospital or anyone else, because the lock is in the product code (right lane). result.title_plain: Clinical state machines and safety rules
result.purpose_plain: Every clinical object in the hospital moves through a strict list of allowed steps: an order, a medication dose, a lab specimen, a result, a bed, a patient visit, an appointment and an insurance claim. Each step has named rules that must all be true before the step can happen. The software can only take steps that are written down, so it cannot skip a safety check such as scanning the patient's wristband: no step exists that leaves the check out. A tool turns these written rules into program code and into automatic tests that try about 1,000 random sequences of actions on each object, to show that no rule can be bypassed.

showcases.title: One guard rule: the high-alert double check (SI-13)
showcases.caption: The YAML writes the rule highAlertCheckSatisfied in plain words: "the dose is not high-alert, or an independent double check is recorded for it (SI-13) … recorded by a second user who is not the administering user, authenticated in their own right (badge and PIN) and privileged to double-check, who attested that patient, product and dose agree with the order". Line 219 of the same file implements it as "not high-alert, or doubleCheckValid". The excerpt below (lines 461-483) shows the detail. A drug whose high-alert flag is unknown is treated as high-alert. The check must be for this dose and this product scan, recorded within the time window, by a different user who is authenticated, privileged and attested. Hand-written and uncommitted; the Gradle unit-test run was still queued.

private fun isHighAlert(facts: MedicationAdministrationFacts): Boolean {
        val scan = facts.scans.product as? ProductScan.Identified
        val productFlagSetOrUnknown = scan != null && facts.configuration.formulary[scan.productId]?.highAlert != false
        return facts.order.orderableHighAlert != false || productFlagSetOrUnknown
    }

    private fun doubleCheckValid(facts: MedicationAdministrationFacts): Boolean {
        val check = facts.doubleCheck
        val commandTime = facts.context.envelope?.issuedAt
        val window = facts.configuration.doubleCheckWindow
        return check != null &&
            commandTime != null &&
            window != null &&
            check.doseId == facts.dose.doseId &&
            checkerIndependent(check, facts) &&
            checkNamesThisSupply(check, facts) &&
            recordedWithinWindow(check.recordedAt, commandTime, window)
    }

    private fun checkerIndependent(
        check: DoubleCheck,
        facts: MedicationAdministrationFacts,
    ): Boolean = check.checkerUserId != facts.actor.userId && check.checkerAuthenticated && check.checkerPrivileged && check.attested

result.title_plain: Design system, patient banner and client shells
result.purpose_plain: The design system is the shared toolkit for how screens look and behave. Every screen of the hospital system is built from it, so buttons, numbers, dialogs and layouts work the same way in Sorani Kurdish, Arabic and English, with right-to-left layout for Kurdish and Arabic. Its centrepiece is the patient banner, the strip at the top of every clinical screen that always shows who the patient is: two identifiers (record number and date of birth), the name in Kurdish, Arabic and Latin script, the photo, allergies, code status, isolation and a dated weight. This matters because treating the wrong patient can kill. Around the banner it supplies one sign and co-sign pattern that checks the patient's identity again when someone signs soon after switching patients, a keyboard command palette, compact and comfortable density modes, and a device layer with a label-printer simulator, so every workstation handles printers, scanners and badge readers the same way.

showcases.caption: The rule that guards signing, in the code's own words. If the patient in this window changed 60 seconds ago or less, signing first asks "Is this the right patient?". Exactly 60.000 s still counts as recent. If the change time is unknown or the clock can't be read, the code assumes the change was recent, so it fails safe. A hospital may make the window longer but never shorter. These are two excerpts from the same file (lines 40-44 and 271-278), committed in 037b572 and used by the sign dialog committed in 9756d2c. result.purpose_plain: This is the part of the hospital system that prints wristbands, specimen labels, receipts, queue tokens and documents. Every patient print must carry two identifiers and the name in the patient's own script plus Latin. A name is never cut off, and the barcode must match the printed text, so staff do not treat or label the wrong patient. Kurdish and Arabic letters must join correctly or names print garbled, every print must say who printed it and be recorded, and patient data must never leave the hospital to be printed.

showcases.title: A synthetic wristband from the PDF renderer
showcases.caption: A 150 x 25 mm wristband, rendered from the renderer's hand-written self-test fixture and rasterised at 150 dpi. It shows the name in Sorani script and in Latin, the MRN, the approximate date of birth, a DataMatrix barcode, the short print mark and the SYNTHETIC notice. An independent decoder (zxing-cpp) read the barcode back as HMS1|M:SYN-000123-7|E:SYN-E-000045|B:SYN-J-000001, which is MRN plus encounter plus band serial (build/docrender-golden/check2.json: pass). Caveats: the image was made on the Windows host on 19 Oct at 08:03, sits in an uncommitted scratch folder, is approved only by the build agent, and still needs a human script review. It is also out of date: the fixture was corrected later so the date prints as '~1990' under 'DOB · Approx.', and this image still shows the older '1990'. This is the PDF path. Zebra printers get ZPL instead.

showcases.title: A synthetic receipt in Arabic, Sorani and Latin
showcases.caption: An 80 mm receipt from the same renderer's self-test fixture. It has joined Arabic and Sorani lines, the Latin name and MRN, amounts printed exactly as given (IQD) and a Code 128 barcode that decodes back to SYN-S-000077. This image still matches its fixture: the fixture's SHA-256 400225a8… equals the manifest. It is uncommitted, in a scratch build folder, agent-approved only, and waiting for a Sorani and Arabic reader to sign it off. Receipt printers get the same picture as an ESC/POS raster image, because ESC/POS code pages cannot shape Sorani.

showcases.title: Layout and content rules for patient prints
showcases.caption: Each rule, why it matters, and where the uncommitted code enforces and tests it. A rule that fails means a refusal, never a partial print. All paths are under backend/modules/platform-docs/src/ unless another folder is named.
